common_name: Guelph Millennium Asparagus (High-Yield Cold-Hardy All-Male Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant 1-year-old crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared trench in early spring; Guelph Millennium breaks dormancy a bit later than older varieties, which helps it dodge late spring frosts, and it establishes an unusually dense, productive root system over its first two non-harvest years.

directions: Plant crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared, well-drained trench in full sun, and resist harvesting at all during the first year to let the fern grow and build root reserves. Guelph Millennium is an all-male hybrid developed at the University of Guelph in Ontario and has become the standard replacement for the older Jersey series across much of North America, valued for exceptionally high, concentrated spear yield, uniform smooth green spears with tight tips, and a root system that establishes unusually quickly for a full-sized harvest by year three. Its later spring emergence than most varieties is an advantage in regions with unpredictable late frosts, since fewer emerging spears are lost to cold snaps. Harvest lightly in year two, moderately in year three, and the full six-to-eight-week season from year four onward, snapping or cutting spears at soil level once they reach 6–8 inches.
sources: University of Guelph — Vineland Research and Innovation Centre asparagus breeding program

common_name: Précoce d'Argenteuil Asparagus (Classic Early French Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared trench in early spring; Précoce d'Argenteuil is an old open-pollinated heirloom rather than an all-male hybrid, so expect some female plants among the seedlings that will bear seed and require weeding out of volunteer seedlings over time.

directions: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, forgoing any harvest in the first year to build the root system. Précoce d'Argenteuil is a classic 19th-century French heirloom named for the asparagus-growing town of Argenteuil near Paris, historically prized for thick, tender spears with purple-tinged tips that emerge notably earlier in spring than most varieties, giving the earliest asparagus harvest of the season. Because it is an open-pollinated variety rather than a modern all-male hybrid, yields run lower than modern hybrids and plantings include both male and female plants, with the females producing red berries in summer that should be removed before they scatter volunteer seedlings through the bed. It remains popular with heirloom growers and in traditional French cuisine for its rich, distinctive flavor; harvest spears once they reach 6–8 inches by snapping or cutting at soil level.

planting.note: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring while still dormant, in deep, fertile soil in full sun; Valentine needs a real winter chill to break dormancy vigorously each year and struggles in mild-winter climates like the Gulf South.

directions: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, in full sun. Valentine is a widely grown American rhubarb variety valued for producing thick, deep-red stalks with good color even in the first year or two after planting, when many other rhubarb varieties are still mostly green, and for a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that holds up well in pies, sauces, and preserves. It is a heavy, dependable producer of large stalks on vigorous plants, and the color intensifies further with consistent cold winters and full sun exposure. Harvest by pulling individual outer stalks with a firm twist rather than cutting, leave at least a third of the stalks on the plant at all times to keep it vigorous, and always discard the leaves, which contain oxalic acid and are not safe to eat.
